title: Motion & Newton's Laws
intro: How do we describe motion, and what makes things move? Learn speed, velocity, acceleration, momentum, force, mass versus weight, why astronauts float, and Newton's three laws of motion, including the simple formulas you will use in calculations.

sections.title: Newton and one set of laws

img.alt: Painted portrait of Sir Isaac Newton with long hair.

steps.title: Newton joins Earth and the heavens
bullets: Sir Isaac Newton (1642 to 1727) realized that the **same physical laws** that work on Earth also work in the heavens.
The word universe comes from a Latin phrase meaning "turned into one". That is exactly Newton's idea: one universe, one set of rules.
He found the **laws of motion** and the law of gravity, and did much more: experiments with light, the first reflecting telescope, and calculus.

img.alt: An old open page showing the title Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica.

steps.title: Where the laws were published
bullets: Newton published his laws of motion and gravity in 1687 in a work called the Principia (Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica).
He listed three laws that apply to all motion, from a ball in your hand to planets, stars and galaxies.

boxes.text: Before Newton, people (following Aristotle) believed the heavens obeyed rules totally different from Earth's. Newton saw an apple fall and realized the gravity pulling the apple is the same pull that holds the Moon in orbit. That one idea removed the wall between Earth and sky.
Universe = "turned into one". One universe, one rulebook.

Slide 1 of the Ch4.1 deck shows a photo of a man on a bicycle; it is NOT Newton (the portrait on slide 2 is). The apple story (1666), the 1687 date and Aristotle are from the textbook (4.2), not from the slides.

sourceNotes: Textbook 4.2 (How did Newton change our view of the universe?), pp. 114-115

images.alt: Painted portrait of Sir Isaac Newton with long hair.

sections.title: Speed and velocity

img.alt: A red car seen from above with a red label that says speed 50 kph.

steps.title: Speed has no direction
bullets: **Speed** = how fast an object moves. speed = Δdistance / Δtime. Base unit: meters per second (m/s).
The car is labelled "50 kph". That number alone is a speed, because it says nothing about which way the car is going.

img.alt: The same red car with a yellow arrow pointing east and the label velocity 50 kph, due east.

steps.title: Velocity has a direction
bullets: **Velocity** = speed with direction attached. The car is going "50 kph, due east", and the yellow arrow shows the direction.
Other velocity examples: 10 m/s due west; 25 m/s at 30° east of north; or in numbers (20, 10) m/s. A velocity always says how fast AND which way.

steps.title: Reading the delta sign
bullets: The triangle Δ just means "change in". So Δdistance is how far you went and Δtime is how long it took.
Example: 150 m in 30 s gives 150 / 30 = 5 m/s.

boxes.text: Direction matters in physics because two objects with the same speed but different directions are doing different things: one is heading toward you and one is heading away. Velocity keeps that information.
Velocity = Very specific (speed + the way you are going). Speed alone is just a number.
Exam wording: "50 km/h" is a speed, "50 km/h due east" is a velocity. The slide's yellow arrow on the car marks the direction. The slide gives units both in m/s and in kph; the base unit is m/s.

sourceNotes: Slide 3 figure: red car with arrow (no legend text beyond the red labels)

images.alt: A red car seen from above with a red label that says speed 50 kph.
The same red car with a yellow arrow pointing east and the label velocity 50 kph, due east.

img.alt: Red cars at three moments with blue and yellow arrows showing speeding up east in the top row and slowing down in the bottom row.

steps.title: Speeding up and slowing down
bullets: **Acceleration** = how quickly an object changes its velocity. acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime. Base unit: meters per second per second (m/s²).
Top row: the car starts at rest and its velocity arrow (yellow) gets longer each moment, so it speeds up with a **positive acceleration** (blue arrow points east).
Bottom row: the car moves east but its velocity arrow shrinks to nothing, so it slows down. Slowing down is a **negative acceleration**.

img.alt: Three strips of a car shown at several moments: speeding up from 30 to 60 km/h, turning at a steady 60 km/h, and slowing from 60 km/h to 0 at a stop sign.

steps.title: Three ways to accelerate
bullets: Speeding up from 30 to 60 km/h is acceleration, because the velocity increases.
Turning at a steady 60 km/h is also acceleration, because the direction of the velocity changes even though the speed does not.
Slowing from 60 km/h to 0 at a stop sign is **negative acceleration**, because the velocity decreases.

img.alt: Red cars on a curved path, each with a yellow arrow along its path and a blue arrow pointing inward toward the center.

steps.title: Turning is acceleration too
bullets: Changing direction counts as acceleration, because velocity changes whenever its direction changes, even if the speed does not.
For an object moving in a circle, the acceleration arrow (blue) points toward the **center of the circle**. The car is always accelerating toward the center.
The yellow arrow along the path is the velocity. It keeps turning, which is why the blue arrow is needed.

boxes.text: Velocity is a speed plus a direction, so it changes when either one changes. A car that goes around a roundabout at a steady 50 km/h still has a changing velocity, so it is accelerating. You feel it as being pushed to the outside of the turn.
Think of the gas pedal, the brake and the steering wheel: all three are "accelerators" because each one changes your velocity.

Common wrong answer: "constant speed means no acceleration". Wrong for a circle. Practice Test 2 Q7 and the slide say turning is acceleration. Also, slide 4 gives no colour legend. Reading slide 4 together with slide 5 (where the blue arrow points to the circle's center), yellow = velocity and blue = acceleration. This is an inference from the pictures, not stated on the slide.

images.alt: Red cars at three moments with blue and yellow arrows showing speeding up east in the top row and slowing down in the bottom row.
Three strips of a car shown at several moments: speeding up from 30 to 60 km/h, turning at a steady 60 km/h, and slowing from 60 km/h to 0 at a stop sign.
Red cars on a curved path, each with a yellow arrow along its path and a blue arrow pointing inward toward the center.

img.alt: A person drops a ball from the roof of a tall building; labels show speed 0 at the start, about 10 m/s after 1 s and about 20 m/s after 2 s.

steps.title: Falling objects speed up steadily
bullets: All falling objects accelerate at very nearly the **same rate** if we ignore air resistance.
On Earth, the speed of a falling object increases by **9.81 m/s** with each additional second: g = 9.81 m/s².
The picture shows speed rising by about 10 m/s every second (0, then about 10, then about 20 m/s). Gravity does not affect the sideways (horizontal) velocity.

steps.title: Why a feather seems slower
bullets: A feather floats down while a rock plummets only because of **air resistance**. With no air (on the Moon), both fall at exactly the same rate.
Galileo showed this idea: gravity accelerates all objects by the same amount, regardless of mass.

boxes.text: A pull from gravity is a steady force. A steady force means a steady acceleration, so the speed grows by the same amount every second: about 9.81 m/s after 1 s, 19.62 m/s after 2 s, 29.43 m/s after 3 s.
"Speed grows by about ten each second" is a good quick rule: 10, 20, 30, 40 ... (exact value 9.81).

Slide 6 text says g = 9.81 m/s^2, but its own picture rounds this to about 10 m/s each second, and the textbook says 9.8 m/s^2 (about 10). Use 9.81 when a question asks for exact numbers and tells you g. At the top of a thrown ball's path the velocity is zero, but gravity still pulls, so the acceleration is still about 9.81 m/s^2 downward (Practice questions Q10).

images.alt: A person drops a ball from the roof of a tall building; labels show speed 0 at the start, about 10 m/s after 1 s and about 20 m/s after 2 s.

sections.title: Mass, inertia and momentum

img.alt: Two carts approach and collide; the system's total momentum remains the same when external forces are negligible.

bullets: **Mass** (symbol m) = how much matter there is in an object.
**Inertia** = how hard it is to accelerate an object. It depends only on mass and is the same thing as mass. There is no separate formula for inertia.

steps.title: Momentum: mass times velocity
bullets: **Momentum** = in everyday terms, how hard it is to stop a moving object. momentum = mass × velocity, or p = mv. Base unit: kg·m/s.
A stationary object has **no momentum**, because its velocity is zero.
Example: a 1200 kg car moving at 25 m/s has p = 1200 × 25 = 30,000 kg·m/s.

steps.title: Truck versus bug
bullets: A bug and a 2-ton truck hit a windshield at the same velocity. The truck has far more momentum because its mass is far bigger, so it hands far more momentum to the car and does far more damage.
Worked numbers: truck 2000 kg, bug 0.0005 kg, same velocity. Momentum ratio = 2000 / 0.0005 = 4,000,000 to 1.
Same speed does not mean same momentum. Mass matters just as much as velocity.

boxes.text: A loaded truck is much harder to stop than a bicycle going the same speed because its mass is much bigger. Momentum bundles both ideas: more mass or more velocity means more momentum and more effort to stop it.
Momentum = "mass in motion". Zero velocity means zero momentum, no matter how heavy.

Inertia is NOT a force and has no formula (slide 7 says so). Also, momentum uses velocity, so it points in a direction. The textbook's bug-versus-truck example: same velocity, but the 2-ton truck has far more momentum than the bug.

sourceNotes: Truck-versus-bug idea: Textbook 4.1 p. 112 (collision example). The 0.0005 kg bug mass is an assumed value (outside source).

sections.title: Force and net force

img.alt: Equal opposing forces balance on one cart, while a greater force in one direction accelerates another.

steps.title: A push or a pull
bullets: **Force** = in everyday terms, a push or a pull. Net forces change an object's momentum, which generally makes the object (a mass) accelerate.
**Force = mass × acceleration**, written F = ma. Base unit: the **newton**, where 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

steps.title: Net force is the total
bullets: The **net force** is all the individual forces added together. Only a net force that is not zero changes momentum.
A car at constant velocity still has forces on it (engine, air resistance, road friction), but they cancel, so the net force is zero.

steps.title: Worked examples with F = ma
bullets: Unit check: 1 kg × 10 m/s² = 10 kg·m/s² = 10 N.
A 55 kg person on a chair that is pulled away accelerates down at 9.8 m/s². Net force = 55 × 9.8 = 539 N, which is her weight.
Turn it around: a = F / m. A 60 N push on a 12 kg object gives 60 / 12 = 5 m/s².

boxes.text: Newton's unit follows from F = ma: 1 kg accelerating at 1 m/s² needs a force of 1 kg × 1 m/s² = 1 kg·m/s², which is called 1 newton. Example: 1500 kg × 2 m/s² = 3000 N.
F = ma triangle: cover the one you want. Force is on top, m and a sit below. Cover m to get m = F / a; cover a to get a = F / m. Example: 60 N on 12 kg gives a = 60 / 12 = 5 m/s².

"There is a force" does not mean "momentum changes". Only the NET force matters (textbook 4.1: a driver pressing the gas exactly cancels friction, so velocity stays constant). Slide 9 uses "Net forces change an object's momentum".

sourceNotes: Worked examples: Textbook Mathematical Insight 4.1 p. 116 (1 kg at 10 m/s², chair pulled away); the 55 kg numbers are made for this site (outside source).

sections.title: Mass versus weight

steps.title: Weight is a force
bullets: **Mass** = amount of matter in an object. **Weight** = the force of gravity acting on an object.
weight = mass × acceleration of gravity, or **F = mg**. Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons.
Example on Earth: 70 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 686.7 N.

img.alt: Four elevator drawings with a person on a scale: the scale reads normal, higher, lower and zero when the cable breaks.

steps.title: Weight versus apparent weight
bullets: **Apparent weight** = the reaction force you feel, resulting from your weight (what a bathroom scale reads).
Elevator at constant velocity: normal. Accelerating up: you weigh more. Accelerating down: you weigh less. Cable breaks (free-fall): you are weightless.
Your mass never changes in any of these cases; only the force the floor exerts on you changes.

steps.title: Worked example: scale in an elevator
bullets: A 70 kg man stands on a scale in an elevator that accelerates upward at 2 m/s². The floor pushes up with a force N, and the net force upward is N - mg = ma.
So N = m(g + a) = 70 × (9.8 + 2) = 70 × 11.8 = **826 N**. His true weight is still mg = 686 N; only the scale reading rises.
If the elevator accelerated downward at 2 m/s², the scale would read 70 × (9.8 - 2) = 546 N.

boxes.text: The scale does not feel gravity directly. It measures how hard the floor pushes up on you. If the elevator accelerates upward, the floor must push harder, so the reading goes up. If you fall freely with the floor, it pushes with no force at all, so the reading is zero.
Mass = "how much stuff" and never changes. Weight = "how hard gravity pulls" and changes from planet to planet. Apparent weight = "what the scale shows".

Slide 11 says weight is the force of gravity and apparent weight is the reaction force felt. The textbook text calls the scale reading "weight (or apparent weight)" and mentions in a footnote that some texts split it into "true weight" (due only to gravity) and "apparent weight". They are saying the same thing. On the exam: moving at CONSTANT speed in an elevator, even downward, the scale reads your normal weight. Only acceleration changes it (Practice questions Q11, Practice Test 2 Q8).

sourceNotes: Textbook 4.1 pp. 113-114 (Figure 4.4; footnote); Mathematical Insight 4.1 p. 116
ASTR207 Practice questions Q11; Practice Test 2 Q8
Elevator numbers are made for this site from F = ma (outside source); the idea is in Textbook 4.1 (Figure 4.4).

images.alt: Four elevator drawings with a person on a scale: the scale reads normal, higher, lower and zero when the cable breaks.

sections.title: Why astronauts are weightless

img.alt: Earth with a tall tower and a curved path showing a person falling around the planet in orbit.

steps.title: Falling around Earth
bullets: There **is** gravity in space. Weightlessness is not an absence of gravity forces; it is an absence of feeling something pushing on you that opposes them.
The picture: the faster you run off the tower, the farther you go before landing. With a rocket giving enough speed, you could keep "falling" around Earth, which is an **orbit**.
Astronauts are in constant free-fall, so nothing pushes back on them and they feel (apparent-)weightless.

steps.title: Quick recap of everything so far
bullets: Speed = Δdistance / Δtime. Speed and direction give velocity. Acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime. Momentum = mass × velocity.
Net forces cause changes in momentum, which gives accelerations. Mass measures matter and weight is the force of gravity.

boxes.text: If gravity vanished in space, the Moon and the space station would fly off in straight lines. They orbit because gravity keeps pulling them. They are weightless because they and everything in them fall together, so no floor or scale pushes up on anyone.
Orbit = "throw yourself at the ground and miss". You keep falling toward Earth but move sideways fast enough that the ground curves away.

Wrong answer to expect: "astronauts are weightless because there is no gravity in space." The textbook says gravity at the space station's altitude (about 350 km) is only about 10% weaker than at the surface, and the speed needed to orbit there is about 28,000 km/h. Those two numbers come from the textbook, not the slides.

sourceNotes: Textbook 4.1 pp. 113-115 (Figure 4.5; Common Misconceptions: No Gravity in Space?)

images.alt: Earth with a tall tower and a curved path showing a person falling around the planet in orbit.

img.alt: Three pictures with captions: a spaceship coasting, a baseball pitcher throwing, and a rocket launching, one for each law of motion.

steps.title: The three laws at a glance
bullets: **First law:** an object moves at constant velocity unless a net force acts to change its speed or direction. Example: a spaceship needs no fuel to keep moving in space.
**Second law:** force = mass × acceleration. Example: a baseball speeds up while the pitcher's arm pushes it.
**Third law:** for any force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. Example: a rocket is pushed up by the gas it throws out the back.

img.alt: A space probe with a large dish coasting through space with the Milky Way behind it.

steps.title: No net force, no change in motion
bullets: **First law:** a body remains at rest, or in motion at a constant speed in a straight line, unless it is acted on by a **net force**.
The recap puts it as: objects move at a constant velocity if no net force is acting on them.
The space probe in the picture needs no fuel to keep going once launched, because nothing is slowing it down.

boxes.text: A rolling car stops on Earth because friction and air resistance are net forces slowing it. Remove them (in space) and the car would keep going forever. That is why spacecraft and astronomical objects need no fuel to keep moving.
Lazy law: things keep doing what they were doing (sitting still, or moving in a straight line at steady speed) until something pushes.

Slide 2 says "constant speed in a straight line", slide 5 and the textbook say "constant velocity". These mean the same thing, because constant velocity includes both steady speed and unchanging direction. First-law exam trap: a gas-off spacecraft in deep space does NOT slow or stop (Practice questions Q13). Also, a smooth plane flight feels like standing still because there is no net force and no acceleration.

images.alt: Three pictures with captions: a spaceship coasting, a baseball pitcher throwing, and a rocket launching, one for each law of motion.
A space probe with a large dish coasting through space with the Milky Way behind it.

sections.title: Newton's second law

img.alt: A baseball player in a gray uniform about to throw a ball.

steps.title: Force makes things accelerate
bullets: **Second law**, two ways to say it: Force = mass × acceleration, or Force = **rate of change in momentum**.
The same push gives a small mass a big acceleration and a large mass a small acceleration. A pitcher's arm accelerates a baseball more than it accelerates a heavy shot-put ball.
Rate of change in momentum means Δmomentum / Δtime: change momentum faster and the force is bigger.

img.alt: Two overhead views of a person swinging a ball on a string: with the string intact the ball circles, and when the string breaks it flies off in a straight line.

steps.title: Turning needs a force too
bullets: A ball on a string is accelerating even at steady speed, because its direction keeps changing. By F = ma the string must pull the ball **inward**.
If the string breaks, the force is gone and the ball flies off in a straight line at constant velocity (first law).
The same idea holds for a car on a curve (tire friction pulls it inward) and a planet (gravity pulls it inward). A heavier vehicle on the same curve needs the bigger force.

steps.title: Worked example: rocket thrust
bullets: A rocket throws out 2 kg of gas every second at 3000 m/s. The gas gains 2 × 3000 = 6000 kg·m/s of momentum each second, so the force is F = Δp / Δt = 6000 N.
By the third law the gas pushes the rocket forward with the same 6000 N. For a 1500 kg rocket, a = F / m = 6000 / 1500 = **4 m/s²**.

boxes.text: F = ma is a recipe: a is what you get when you divide the net force by the mass. Double the mass and the acceleration is cut in half; double the force and the acceleration doubles. Example: a momentum change of 12 kg·m/s in 0.04 s needs F = 12 / 0.04 = 300 N.
Heavy things are lazy: the bigger the mass, the smaller the acceleration for the same push.

The two forms of the second law are the same law. Use F = ma when mass is steady and F = Δp/Δt when momentum changes. The textbook uses the baseball and the shot put. Practice Test 2 Q7 (car vs truck on a roundabout): same speed means same acceleration, so the truck has the bigger FORCE, not the bigger acceleration.

sourceNotes: ASTR207 Practice questions Q12; Practice Test 2 Q7
Rocket thrust numbers are made for this site from F = Δp/Δt (outside source). Figure 4.7 and the string example: Textbook 4.2 p. 117.

images.alt: A baseball player in a gray uniform about to throw a ball.
Two overhead views of a person swinging a ball on a string: with the string intact the ball circles, and when the string breaks it flies off in a straight line.

sections.title: Newton's third law

img.alt: A space shuttle lifting off with bright flame and a cloud of smoke at the base.

steps.title: Every push has a push back
bullets: **Third law:** for every force there is always an **equal and opposite reaction force**.
A rocket engine drives hot gas out the back. The gas pushes back on the rocket with an equal and opposite force, and that force moves the rocket forward.
Standing still: your weight pushes down on the ground, and the ground pushes up on you with an equal force.

steps.title: Equal forces, unequal accelerations
bullets: You pull on Earth with exactly the same force that Earth pulls on you, but opposite in direction.
Your mass is tiny compared to Earth's, so the same force gives you a large acceleration and Earth an unnoticeable one. That is why you fall toward Earth and Earth does not visibly rise to meet you.

steps.title: Worked example: rifle recoil
bullets: A 4.0 kg rifle pushes a 0.020 kg bullet forward with 2000 N. The bullet pushes back on the rifle with the same 2000 N (third law).
Bullet: a = 2000 / 0.020 = 100,000 m/s². Rifle: a = 2000 / 4.0 = 500 m/s². Equal forces, but the light bullet accelerates 200 times more.
That backward push on the rifle is the "kick" you feel.

boxes.text: The rocket does not push against the ground. It pushes on its own exhaust gas, and the gas pushes back. That is why a rocket works even in empty space where there is nothing to push against.
Forces come in pairs, like handshakes: you cannot shake hands with one person pushing only.

Practice Test 2 Q10: Newton's third law applies in ALL cases (very different masses, forces at a distance such as gravity, microscopic objects, many objects). "Equal forces" does not mean "equal accelerations" (F = ma gives different accelerations for different masses). Common misconception from the textbook: a rocket does NOT push off the ground.

sourceNotes: Textbook 4.2 p. 117 (Newton's Third Law; Common Misconceptions: What Makes a Rocket Launch?)
Practice Test 2 Q10 and its explanation

quiz.q:
Which of these cars is accelerating?
I. A car on a straight, flat road at a steady 50 mph.
II. A car on a straight uphill road at a steady 30 mph.
III. A car going around a circular track at a steady 100 mph.
quiz.why: Acceleration means the velocity (speed or direction) is changing. In I and II the car holds a steady speed in a straight line, so its velocity is constant. In III the direction keeps changing, so the car accelerates even at constant speed.
quiz.source: Textbook Quick Quiz 1; Ch4.1 slides 4-5

quiz.q: A car drives at a steady 72 km/h. How far does it travel in 15 s? (Convert to m/s first.)
quiz.why: 72 km/h = 72,000 m / 3600 s = 20 m/s. Distance = speed × time = 20 m/s × 15 s = 300 m. Using 72 directly with seconds gives 1,080 m, a units mistake.
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slide 3 (speed, base unit m/s). Numbers made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A car moving at 12 m/s speeds up with a steady acceleration of 2.5 m/s² for 6 s. What is its speed at the end?
quiz.why: Gain in speed = acceleration × time = 2.5 × 6 = 15 m/s. Final speed = starting speed + gain = 12 + 15 = 27 m/s. Forgetting the starting speed gives 15 m/s.
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slide 4 (acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime). Numbers made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A driver traveling at 60 miles per hour slams on the brakes. If the acceleration averages -20 miles per hour per second, how long does the car take to stop?
quiz.why: time = Δvelocity / acceleration = (0 - 60) / (-20) = 3 s. Dividing 20 by 60 (0.33 s) turns the formula upside down.
quiz.source: Textbook Exercise 42c (Units of Acceleration); Ch4.1 slide 4

quiz.q: A rock is dropped from rest from the roof of a tall building, as in the picture. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 9.8 m/s², how fast is it falling 4 s after it is released?
quiz.why: Speed grows by 9.8 m/s every second, so after 4 s: v = 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 m/s. The picture shows the same pattern (about 10 m/s after 1 s, about 20 m/s after 2 s). Squaring the time would wrongly give 156.8 m/s.
quiz.source: Textbook 4.1 Fig. 4.2 and Exercise 42a (textbook rounds g to 10 m/s^2, giving 40 m/s); Ch4.1 slide 6

img.alt: A person drops a ball from the roof of a tall building; labels show speed 0 at the start, about 10 m/s after 1 s and about 20 m/s after 2 s.

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 29.4 m/s. Take up as positive, use g = 9.8 m/s² and ignore air resistance. What is the ball's velocity 5 s after the throw?
options: 0 m/s, because the ball stopped at the top
quiz.why: Gravity changes the velocity by -9.8 m/s every second, so over 5 s the change is -9.8 × 5 = -49 m/s. New velocity = 29.4 - 49 = -19.6 m/s: the ball reached the top after 3 s and is now coming down. It does not stay at rest at the top because gravity keeps accelerating it.
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slides 4 and 6; Textbook 4.1 (acceleration of gravity). Numbers made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its path, which statement is TRUE?
options: Its velocity is zero, but it is still accelerating downward at about 9.81 m/s².
Its velocity and its acceleration are both zero.
Its velocity is at its maximum.
No forces act on it at that instant.
quiz.why: Gravity keeps pulling the ball with the same force the whole time, so the acceleration is about 9.81 m/s² downward even when the velocity is momentarily zero.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q10; Ch4.1 slide 6

quiz.q:
Rank these moving carts from the GREATEST to the LEAST momentum.
A. 2 kg moving at 6 m/s
B. 0.5 kg moving at 30 m/s
C. 20 kg moving at 0.5 m/s
D. 3 kg moving at 3 m/s
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slide 8. Numbers made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A 2-ton truck (about 2000 kg) and a 0.5 g bug (0.0005 kg) hit a windshield with the same velocity. How many times more momentum does the truck have?
quiz.why: The velocities are equal, so the momentum ratio equals the mass ratio: 2000 / 0.0005 = 4,000,000. (Only 4,000 if you forget to change grams into kilograms.)
quiz.source: Textbook 4.1 p. 112 (bug versus 2-ton truck); Ch4.1 slide 8. Bug mass made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A 55 kg person stands on a chair that is suddenly pulled out from under her. At the first instant she accelerates downward at 9.8 m/s². What net force acts on her?
quiz.why: F = ma = 55 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 539 N. This net force is just the force of gravity on her, her true weight. Dividing (55 / 9.8 = 5.6) is a common slip.
quiz.source: Textbook Mathematical Insight 4.1 p. 116 (chair pulled away); Ch4.1 slides 9-10. Mass made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A pitcher's arm applies the same net force to a 0.15 kg baseball and to a 7.5 kg shot put. How does the baseball's acceleration compare with the shot put's?
options: The same, because the force is the same
quiz.why: a = F / m, so with the same force the accelerations are in the inverse ratio of the masses: 7.5 / 0.15 = 50. The lighter ball accelerates 50 times more.
quiz.source: Ch4.2 slide 3; Textbook 4.2 p. 116 (baseball and shot put). Masses made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: The same net force is applied to a 2 kg cart and a 4 kg cart. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The 2 kg cart accelerates twice as much as the 4 kg cart.
Both carts have the same acceleration because the force is the same.
The 4 kg cart accelerates twice as much as the 2 kg cart.
The 2 kg cart accelerates four times as much as the 4 kg cart.
Neither cart accelerates unless the force is larger than its weight.
quiz.why: a = F / m. The same force on half the mass gives double the acceleration.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q12; Ch4.2 slide 3

quiz.q:
Which of these statements about F = ma are TRUE?
I. If the same net force acts on twice the mass, the acceleration is half as large.
II. If the net force on an object doubles, its acceleration doubles.
III. An object whose acceleration is zero must have no forces acting on it.
quiz.why: a = F / m, so I and II are true. III is false: zero acceleration means the NET force is zero, which can happen when several forces cancel (a car at constant velocity still has engine force and friction).
quiz.source: Ch4.2 slide 3; Ch4.1 slide 9; Textbook 4.1 p. 112 (net force)

quiz.q: A 70 kg man stands on a scale in an elevator, as in the picture, while the elevator accelerates upward at 2 m/s². Using g = 9.8 m/s², what does the scale read (his apparent weight)?
quiz.why: The floor pushes up with force N and gravity pulls down with mg, so the net upward force is N - mg = ma. Then N = m(g + a) = 70 × (9.8 + 2) = 70 × 11.8 = 826 N. 686 N is his weight at rest, 546 N is for accelerating downward.
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slides 10-11; Textbook 4.1 Fig. 4.4; F = ma. Numbers made for this site (outside source)

img.alt: Four elevator drawings with a person on a scale: the scale reads normal, higher, lower and zero when the cable breaks.

quiz.q: You stand on a bathroom scale in an elevator that moves downward at a constant speed. What does the scale read?
options: It depends on how fast the elevator is moving
quiz.why: The scale differs from your normal weight only when the elevator is accelerating. At constant velocity there is no net force on you.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q11; Ch4.1 slide 11; Textbook Fig. 4.4

quiz.q: The rope holding an elevator car is pulled upward. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The elevator accelerates upward whatever the pull, and the occupants' true weight increases.
The elevator accelerates upward only if the pull is greater than the weight; the occupants' true weight increases.
The elevator accelerates upward whatever the pull, and the occupants' apparent weight does not change.
The elevator accelerates upward only if the upward pull is greater than the weight; the occupants' true weight does not change, only their apparent weight.
The elevator accelerates upward only if the pull is greater than the weight; both true and apparent weight increase.
quiz.why: A net upward force is needed to accelerate (second law). True weight is the force of gravity (mg) and does not change; the scale reading (apparent weight) rises.
quiz.source: Practice Test 2 Q8 (answer C in explained file); Ch4.1 slides 10-11

quiz.q: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth (g = 9.8 m/s²). On the Moon the acceleration of gravity is 1.6 m/s². What are her mass and weight on the Moon?
quiz.why: Mass is the amount of matter, so it stays 80 kg. Weight = mg = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N (on Earth it would be 80 × 9.8 = 784 N). The 13 kg answer comes from wrongly dividing 128 by 9.8.
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slide 10; Textbook 4.1 p. 113. Moon gravity value given for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: Which person is weightless? (Assume air resistance is negligible.)
options: A scuba diver exploring a deep-sea wreck
An astronaut standing on the Moon
A person on a scale in an elevator moving up at constant speed
A passenger in a rocket during launch
A child in the air during a jump on a trampoline
quiz.why: Weightless means in free-fall, with nothing pushing back on you. The child in the air is in free-fall. The diver is held up by the water, the astronaut on the Moon by the ground, the elevator rider by the floor, and the launch passenger is pressed into the seat even harder.
quiz.source: Textbook Quick Quiz 3; Ch4.1 slides 11-12

quiz.q: A crew member in low Earth orbit feels weightless. Which explanation for this observation is INCORRECT?
options: Gravity keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth.
There is no gravity in space, which is why astronauts float.
An orbiting astronaut is in constant free-fall.
Apparent weight can be zero while the force of gravity is still acting.
Objects in space remain affected by gravity.
quiz.why: Gravity acts everywhere in space. Astronauts float because they are in free-fall, not because gravity is absent.
quiz.source: Ch4.1 slides 12-14; Textbook 4.1 (Common Misconceptions)

quiz.q: A spacecraft in deep space, far from any star or planet, shuts off its engines. What happens?
options: It gradually slows down and stops.
It speeds up because there is no air resistance.
It starts to move in a circle.
It keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.
quiz.why: With no net force, Newton's first law says it keeps its velocity: straight line, constant speed.
quiz.source: ASTR207 Practice questions Q13; Ch4.2 slide 2

quiz.q: An astronaut on a spacewalk floats right beside the Space Station, with no tether, moving at the same velocity as the station. What happens?
options: She stays next to the station, because nothing makes her velocity change
She quickly drifts away, because there is no gravity at that height
She falls straight down to Earth within seconds
She drifts backward, because she is weightless
She stops, because no force pushes her forward
quiz.why: She and the station share the same velocity and both are in free-fall. With no net force changing her velocity relative to the station (first law), she stays alongside. Gravity is still acting (only about 10% weaker there) and it keeps both in orbit.
quiz.source: Textbook Exercise 27 (Does It Make Sense?); Textbook 4.1 and 4.2; Ch4.1 slide 12, Ch4.2 slide 2

quiz.q: In deep space, a 1500 kg rocket's engine throws out 2 kg of gas every second at 3000 m/s. Treat the rocket's mass as constant and ignore gravity. What is the rocket's acceleration?
quiz.why: Force = rate of change in momentum = (2 kg × 3000 m/s) / 1 s = 6000 N on the gas. By the third law the gas pushes the rocket forward with 6000 N. Then a = F / m = 6000 / 1500 = 4 m/s². Forgetting to divide by the mass gives 6,000.
quiz.source: Ch4.2 slides 3-4 (F = rate of change in momentum; third law); Textbook 4.2 (rocket). Numbers made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: A rocket coasting in empty space needs to turn to the left. Which action will work?
options: Fire an engine that shoots gas out to the right
Fire an engine that shoots gas out to the left
Push the nose against the nearest solid surface
Do nothing: changing direction needs no force
Rotate the rocket clockwise without firing any engine
quiz.why: Turning left means the rocket needs a force toward the left. By the third law the force on the rocket is opposite to the force on the gas, so the gas must be shot out to the right. Rotating the rocket does not change its velocity.
quiz.source: Textbook Quick Quiz 5; Ch4.2 slide 4

quiz.q: A small car (mass m) and a large truck (mass M) drive around the same roundabout at the same speed. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The acceleration of the car is greater than that of the truck, since it has less mass.
The acceleration of the truck is greater than that of the car, since it has more mass.
The force on the car is greater than the force on the truck, since it has less mass.
The force on the truck is greater than the force on the car, since it has more mass.
Neither vehicle accelerates, since both move at constant speed.
quiz.why: Same speed in the same circle means the same acceleration (turning is acceleration). F = ma then gives a bigger force for the bigger mass.
quiz.source: Practice Test 2 Q7 (answer D in explained file); Ch4.1 slides 5, 9; Ch4.2 slide 3

quiz.q: A ball is swung in a horizontal circle on a string, as in the picture. At the instant the string breaks, which path does the ball follow?
options: It keeps moving in the same circle
It spirals outward in a curve
A straight line at constant speed, in the direction it was moving at that instant
A straight line toward the center of the circle
A straight line directly away from the center of the circle
quiz.why: The string's inward pull was the only force making the ball turn. Once it is gone there is no net force, so the first law says the ball keeps its velocity: a straight line at the same speed along the direction it was moving at that instant.
quiz.source: Textbook 4.2 Fig. 4.7 p. 117; Ch4.2 slides 2-3

img.alt: Two overhead views of a person swinging a ball on a string: with the string intact the ball circles, and when the string breaks it flies off in a straight line.

quiz.q: Consider Newton's second law, F = ma. If a planet travels in an elliptical orbit, what does that imply about the force acting on the planet?
options: The constant acceleration of the planet, shown by its orbital path, comes from a constant gravitational force acting on it.
Newton's second law does not apply to orbits; Kepler's laws are needed to explain orbital motion.
The varying acceleration of the planet, shown by its orbital path, comes from a varying gravitational force acting on it.
The mass and the acceleration of the planet vary over the orbit so that the gravitational force stays constant.
No force acts on the planet, which is why it does not slow down or speed up in its orbit.
quiz.why: On an ellipse the distance to the Sun keeps changing, so the pull of gravity changes, and with constant mass F = ma gives a changing acceleration. With no force the planet would fly off in a straight line (first law).
quiz.source: Practice Test 2 Q9 (answer C in explained file); Ch4.2 slides 3 and 5

quiz.q: In which of the following situations is Newton's third law NOT applicable?
options: None of these; it applies in all cases.
When one object is much more massive than the other.
When the force is gravity and the objects are physically separated.
When more than two objects are involved.
quiz.why: Every force has an equal and opposite reaction force, whatever the masses, distances or number of objects. A big mass difference only changes the accelerations, not the forces.
quiz.source: Practice Test 2 Q10 (answer E in explained file); Ch4.2 slide 4

quiz.q: When you jump off a chair, you and Earth pull on each other with equal and opposite forces, yet you fall toward Earth and Earth does not noticeably move toward you. Why?
options: Earth pulls on you with a bigger force than you pull on it.
The third law does not apply to gravity.
Gravity pulls only on small objects.
Earth's mass is so large that the same force gives it an acceleration too small to notice.
quiz.why: The forces are equal, but a = F / m. A huge mass gives an extremely tiny acceleration.
quiz.source: Ch4.2 slides 3-4; Textbook 4.2 p. 117

quiz.q: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet. While the shot is fired, the rifle pushes the bullet forward with an average force of 2000 N. How do the bullet's acceleration and the rifle's backward acceleration compare?
options: They are the same, because the forces are equal
quiz.why: By the third law the bullet pushes back on the rifle with the same 2000 N. Then a = F / m: bullet 2000 / 0.020 = 100,000 m/s², rifle 2000 / 4.0 = 500 m/s². The ratio is 100,000 / 500 = 200, which is just the mass ratio 4.0 / 0.020.
quiz.source: Ch4.2 slide 4 (third law) and slide 3 (F = ma); rifle example per the course practice material. Numbers made for this site (outside source)

quiz.q: Why can a rocket accelerate in empty space, where there is nothing to push against?
options: The rocket pushes off the ground just before it leaves.
The exhaust gas pushes against the air behind the rocket.
Its engine pushes hot gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward with an equal and opposite force.
Newton's third law does not apply in space.
A rocket needs no force to accelerate in space.
quiz.why: The rocket and its exhaust push on each other (third law). No ground or air is needed.
quiz.source: Ch4.2 slide 4; Textbook 4.2 (What Makes a Rocket Launch?)

order.title: Rank the momentum
order.prompt: Put these moving carts in order from the SMALLEST momentum (bottom) to the GREATEST (top). Remember p = m × v.
order.why: Momentum is mass times velocity: 3 kg at 3 m/s = 9, 20 kg at 0.5 m/s = 10, 1 kg at 11 m/s = 11, 2 kg at 6 m/s = 12, and 0.5 kg at 30 m/s = 15 kg·m/s.

order.title: Same push, different carts
order.prompt: The same 60 N net force pushes each cart. Order them from the SMALLEST acceleration (bottom) to the LARGEST (top).
order.why: a = F / m. With 60 N: 20 kg gives 3 m/s², 12 kg gives 5, 10 kg gives 6, 5 kg gives 12, and 2 kg gives 30 m/s². The lighter the cart, the bigger the acceleration.

order.title: Scale reading in an elevator
order.prompt: Order the elevator situations by what a bathroom scale reads, from the LOWEST (bottom) to the HIGHEST (top).
order.why: In free-fall the floor pushes with no force, so the scale reads zero. Accelerating downward gives less than normal, constant velocity or standing still gives the normal weight, and accelerating upward gives more.

sort.title: Is it accelerating?
sort.prompt: Sort each situation: is the object accelerating or not? (Acceleration means velocity changes, in speed or direction.)

items.text: A car speeding up from 30 to 60 km/h
A car slowing from 60 km/h to a stop
A car going around a curve at a steady 60 km/h
A planet orbiting the Sun
A rock falling freely near Earth
A ball swung in a circle on a string at steady speed
A car on a straight flat road at a steady 50 mph
A smooth airplane flight at constant velocity
An elevator moving down at constant speed
A spacecraft coasting in deep space with its engines off
A parked car

sort.why: Acceleration is any change in velocity. Speeding up, slowing down and turning all change velocity. A steady speed in a straight line (or standing still) means constant velocity, so no acceleration.

sort.title: Which of Newton's laws?
sort.prompt: Sort each example by the law of motion that explains it best.
buckets: First law (no net force, no change)

items.text: A spacecraft keeps coasting with no fuel
A smooth plane flight feels like standing still
A ball on a string flies off straight when the string breaks
A car would roll forever if friction and air were removed
A pitcher's arm speeds up a baseball more than a shot put
A 60 N push gives a 12 kg object 5 m/s²
A heavier vehicle needs a bigger force to take the same curve at the same speed
The same force gives a small mass a big acceleration
Rocket gas pushes the rocket forward
You pull on Earth as hard as Earth pulls on you
The ground pushes up on you as hard as you push down on it
A rocket can speed up in empty space

sort.why: First law: no net force means constant velocity. Second law: net force sets acceleration through F = ma. Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs, which is how a rocket pushes on its own exhaust.

sort.title: Mass or weight?
sort.prompt: Sort each statement: does it describe mass or weight?

items.text: The amount of matter in your body
Measured in kilograms
The same on the Moon as on Earth
Does not change when an elevator accelerates
The same thing as inertia
The force of gravity on an object, F = mg
Measured in newtons
Smaller on the Moon than on Earth
What a bathroom scale reads
Rises on a scale when an elevator accelerates upward

sort.why: Mass is how much matter there is and never changes with place. Weight is a force (mass times the acceleration of gravity), so it changes with gravity and with acceleration, such as in an elevator.
